en: The Sūtra on Śāriputra and Mahāmaudgalyāyana Wandering through the Four Crossroads, translated by the Tripitaka Master Kang Mengxiang of the Western Regions during the Later Han Dynasty.
Thus have I heard: At one time, [the Buddha was] at the Āmalaka Medicine Tree Garden of the Śākya clan in Śrāvastī. At that time,

The venerable Śāriputra and the bhikṣu Mahāmaudgalyāyana, having traveled through various kingdoms for one year together with a great assembly of five hundred bhikṣus, returned to the Medicinal Tree Grove, desiring to see the World-Honored One.
When these people returned, the many bhikṣus conversed with one another; each donned his robes and took up his bowl, their voices rising high and their sounds resonating clearly.
The Buddha, knowing this beforehand, asked the Venerable Ānanda:
"Who is this bhikṣu?
He raises a great sound whose resonance is vast and overflowing, like a fisherman raising his voice as he hauls in a net."
Ānanda said to the Buddha:
“So be it, World-Honored One!

Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana have been traveling through various kingdoms for one year, and together with a great assembly of five hundred bhikṣus, they have arrived at the medicinal tree. There I saw the bhikṣus each engaged in conversation, putting on their robes and taking up their bowls; their voices were loud and their resonance filled the air.”
The Buddha said to Ānanda,
“Do not let the bhikṣus come to me.
Ānanda addressed the Buddha:
"So be it," they replied.

Having received their instructions, they rose from their seats, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, circumambulated him three times, and withdrew. They went to where the bhikṣus Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana were, exchanged greetings with them, stood to one side, and said to the worthy Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana:
"Please do not go to the place of the Buddha; the World-Honored One has given an instruction."

Upon hearing Ānanda’s words, Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana rose from their seats and went to where the Buddha was. They prostrated at his feet, circumambulated him three times, quickly set aside their robes and bowls, and went out to the medicinal tree together with the assembly of bhikṣus.

At that time, the Śākya upāsakas had gathered together to discuss a certain doctrine. Seeing from afar Śāriputra and Mahāmaudgalyāyana accompanied by a multitude of bhikṣus—robed, with bowls in hand, arriving at the foot of the medicinal tree at dawn during the day—they thought, "Five hundred bhikṣus are with them; we should surely go to inquire after their well-being."
At that time, the assembly of Śākya upāsakas immediately rose and went quickly to where Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana were; they prostrated at their feet and withdrew to stand to one side.
At that time, the lay devotees asked Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana:
"For what reason do you put on your robes and take up your bowls to go during the day among the medicinal trees?"
Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana replied to the lay follower of the Śākya clan:
"We have returned from traveling through various countries to join the assembly of bhikṣus; being all exhausted, we are now staying here in the open air."
The lay devotees replied: "O worthy ones!

We have here prepared seats in full and lit lamps for illumination; we only pray that you, along with the assembly of bhikṣus, will deign to come. If it is said that [this is not for] the Buddha, then you may withdraw."

The venerable Śāriputra and Mahāmaudgalyāyana silently assented; they then proceeded to the place where the seat had been prepared, entered the hall, and sat together with the assembly of monks upon their couches.
At that time, the lay devotees of the Śākya clan went to where the Buddha was, prostrated at his feet, joined their palms, and said to the Buddha:
“We entreat the World-Honored One to take pity on us and remain [in this world]. Indeed, O Great Sage!”
I have faith in the community of bhikṣus. Why is this?
Regarding those bhikṣus who have exhausted all outflows and attained arhatship—having accomplished what was to be done—I harbor no doubt.

These bhikṣus likewise have no hesitation; however, there may be bhikṣus who are young, newly trained, and recently ordained, who have not long entered this Dharma and Vinaya, whose minds are still shifting or prone to change—just as when a torrential flood suddenly comes upon the world, there is nothing to obstruct it.
"So it is, World-Honored One!

A newly ordained bhikṣu who has recently entered this Dharma and Vinaya may have a mind that is still shifting or prone to change; fearing that his resolve and conduct might be altered, he does not wish to behold the Great Sage."
At that time, Brahmā descended suddenly and stood before the Buddha with palms joined, saying:
"We beseech the World-Honored One; we implore you with compassion to remain among us. Pray do so, O Great Sage!"
I have faith in the community of bhikṣus. Why is this?
Regarding those among the bhikṣu-saṃgha who have exhausted all outflows and attained arhatship—having accomplished what was to be done—I have no doubt.

These bhikṣus will not be hesitant; however, there may be bhikṣus who are young, newly trained, and have only recently left the household life, who have not long entered this Dharma and Vinaya, and whose minds may shift or undergo change.
The Buddha immediately granted his consent to the Brahma King.
The Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana, with his clairvoyant vision, perceived from afar that the Buddha’s mind had granted his consent, and he requested to behold the Great Sage’s majestic virtue.

It was like a great multi-storied pavilion or a large lecture hall, clean and well-smeared with plaster, with its windows and balconies opened wide. When the sun first rose in the east and entered through the windows, its light shone upon the western wall. The worthy Maudgalyāyana, with his divine eye of transcendent vision, saw from afar the World-Honored One’s majestic and sublime physical marks. Thereupon, Maudgalyāyana addressed the assembly of bhikṣus:
"Virtuous ones!..."
"Rise, put on your robes, take up your bowl, and let each of you, young brahmins, go forth.
The bhikṣu said,
"I shall do as instructed."
He quickly adjusted his robes and, following Śāriputra, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, and the others, went to where the Buddha was. He prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and withdrew to sit to one side.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Śāriputra:
“In previous lives, I also made offerings to the assembly of bhikṣus; what do you think of this?”
Śāriputra thought to himself: "The World-Honored One has long provided for the assembly of bhikṣus.

Among these great sages, the bhikṣus are simple and unadorned; they know moderation in their desires, abide in tranquility, and are resolute in their diligence. The Buddha, the God among Gods, is the Dharma King who tames those who are untamed and causes them to receive his teachings. Yet the movements of this assembly of bhikṣus are light and frivolous; today the Great Sage shows compassion toward the Sangha."
The Buddha said,
"Excellent, excellent, Śāriputra!"
While correctly maintaining this mindfulness to eliminate unwholesome thoughts,
for what reason?
Who among the community of bhikṣus has cast off all heavy burdens?
"Only the Tathāgata’s ear is such that there is nowhere it does not abide, as is the case with Śāriputra and Mahāmaudgalyāyana.
Then the Buddha addressed Mahāmaudgalyāyana, saying:
"What do you think regarding the mind?"
"Who honors the community of bhikṣus?
Who disciplines the community of bhikṣus?
Thus I thought to myself.
"Now, the Buddha, World-Honored One, honors and restrains the assembly of bhikṣus. Indeed, Great Sage!

Among this assembly of bhikṣus, there are some who are simple and have little desire, being content with what they know; or there are those who are incapable, yet claim for themselves that their practice is peaceful, diligent, and unremitting, saying, 'As it is fitting for the Tathāgata, the Dharma King, so should I also be.'"
The Buddha said:
"Cease this thought! Do not harbor such a notion;
you should instead form another thought."
Why is this? In this regard, Maudgalyāyana, who is capable of bearing the removal of all heavy burdens?
Only the Tathāgata, as well as Śāriputra and Mahāmaudgalyāyana.
"Cross the surging flood by means of faith; take heedfulness as your boat.
Cross over suffering and affliction by means of the Noble Truths; cross to the ultimate shore by means of wisdom.

When the Buddha had spoken these words, sixty bhikṣus attained the exhaustion of outflows and liberation of mind; countless other bhikṣus became free from dust and defilement, and the Dharma-eye regarding all phenomena arose within them.
When the Buddha had spoken thus, the bhikṣus, lay devotees, devas, nāgas, and spirits were all filled with joy.
The Sūtra on Śāriputra and Mahāmaudgalyāyana Traveling Through the Four Crossroads.
